strengths: Well-motivated problem: Error recovery and handling execution failures is a critical bottleneck for deploying smaller language models in agentic, multi-turn environments.

Sound and effective methodology: The FISSION-GRPO mechanism smartly transforms zero-reward failed trajectories into productive corrective training instances by conditioning on diagnostic feedback and resampling rollouts on-policy, resolving the vanishing gradient problem in standard GRPO.

Consistent empirical performance: The proposed method yields clear and consistent gains across three scales of the Qwen3 family (1.7B, 4B, 8B) on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn, outperforming standard GRPO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO, and external specialized agents.

Insightful analysis and ablations: The decomposition into one-shot success vs. error recovery rate demonstrates that gains indeed stem from self-correction without compromising base accuracy. The ablation between dynamic and static feedback clearly isolates the value of the learned error simulator.
weaknesses: Narrow benchmark evaluation: Evaluation is conducted exclusively on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn. Testing on additional multi-turn agentic or tool-use benchmarks (e.g., StableToolBench, WebShop, or interactive code execution environments) would substantiate the broader generality of the approach.

Compute and sampling budget fairness: FISSION-GRPO introduces extra rollout sampling ($G'$ per error) and calls to a 32B error simulator during training. The paper lacks a compute-matched baseline comparison (e.g., GRPO with a proportionally larger sample size $G$ or longer exploration budget) and does not report wall-clock/FLOP training overhead.

Reliance on teacher models for the simulator: The error simulator requires supervised fine-tuning on Claude-4-Sonnet generated diagnostics. While effective, this introduces dependency on proprietary teacher models and extra pipeline complexity.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: the vulnerability of smaller language models to repetitive failure loops and state collapse when encountering execution errors in multi-turn tool interaction.

The core methodological concept—fissioning failed trajectories into on-policy corrective groups augmented with synthetic/deterministic environment feedback—is an intuitive and principled way to provide dense corrective supervision within an online RL loop.
Comprehensive empirical gains across three parameter scales of the Qwen3 family (1.7B, 4B, and 8B), consistently outperforming standard GRPO, DAPO, and Dr.GRPO on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn.

Thorough ablation and diagnostic analyses, including decoupling one-shot success from conditional error recovery, comparing static vs. dynamic error feedback, sensitivity analysis on trigger interval N, and detailed qualitative trajectory breakdowns.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to a single benchmark (BFCL v4 Multi-Turn). While BFCL v4 is well-suited because of its multi-turn retry mechanism, demonstrating generalizability across other interactive tool/agent environments (e.g., StableToolBench, InterCode, or web navigation tasks) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

Compute and sample budget matching is not strictly controlled: FISSION-GRPO generates additional rollouts (G' rollouts per flagged error context) beyond the baseline G exploration rollouts. It is unclear whether standard GRPO with an equivalent total rollout or FLOP budget would close part of the performance gap.

The Error Simulator relies on access to ground-truth tool calls during training (S_phi(x, tau_err, tau_gt)) and requires running a Qwen3-32B model during Stage 2. The paper lacks detailed profiling of wall-clock training time overhead and GPU memory footprint incurred by this auxiliary model during the RL loop.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in LLM tool use: the tendency of smaller language models to degenerate into repetitive loops and fail to recover when encountering execution errors in multi-turn interactions.

The proposed FISSION-GRPO framework is conceptually sound and directly tackles the vanishing gradient / zero-reward problem of GRPO on failed rollouts by dynamically branching failed trajectories into recovery rollouts conditioned on diagnostic feedback.

Empirical improvements are consistent across model sizes (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B) on the BFCL v4 Multi-Turn benchmark, outperforming strong RL baselines (GRPO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO) and specialized 8B agent models.

The paper includes informative analytical breakdowns and ablations, specifically isolating the error recovery rate from one-shot success, measuring the benefit of dynamic vs. static simulated feedback, and evaluating the sensitivity of the trigger interval hyperparameter.
The manuscript is well-written and well-structured, with clear figures, comprehensive pseudo-code in the appendix, and transparent prompt templates.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined exclusively to the BFCL v4 Multi-Turn benchmark. Testing across additional multi-turn environments (e.g., interactive coding benchmarks like InterCode or web/API interaction suites like StableToolBench) would substantially strengthen the claims of generalizability.

The training pipeline relies on ground-truth tool calls to synthesize error feedback. As shown in Section 3.3.2 and the prompt template (Figure 5), the Error Simulator takes the ground-truth call as input to formulate its diagnostic message. This restricts the framework to environments where complete ground-truth execution references are available, limiting applicability in open-ended RL setups.

The method introduces noticeable computational and engineering complexity: training an auxiliary 32B error simulator and generating G' additional rollouts per error during RL training. The paper lacks concrete wall-clock time and FLOPs comparisons against baseline GRPO.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Addresses a critical failure mode in small tool-calling LLMs—repetitive hallucination loops following tool execution errors—which standard GRPO cannot easily address due to vanishing intra-group reward variance when all rollouts fail.

Effective framework design: FISSION-GRPO elegantly turns failed trajectories into actionable learning signals by injecting simulated diagnostic feedback and resampling recovery rollouts on-policy, thereby restoring advantage variance and directly optimizing recovery behavior.

Strong empirical results across multiple scales and benchmarks: Demonstrates consistent gains across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B on BFCL v4 Multi-Turn, TAU-Bench, and TAU2-Bench, outperforming standard GRPO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO, and AWPO.

Thorough analysis and ablation studies: The authors provide compute-matched comparisons confirming that improvements do not stem from extra compute budget, analyze feedback quality (static generic prompts vs. dynamic simulator feedback), and conduct both automated and human evaluations (Cohen's kappa = 0.71) to ensure the Error Simulator does not leak ground-truth targets.
weaknesses: The Error Simulator relies on privileged access to the ground-truth tool call (tau_gt) during training to synthesize realistic runtime error messages, restricting the approach to supervised/reference-guided RL environments rather than completely open-ended exploration without ground truth.

Training and inference with the Error Simulator introduces architectural overhead (requiring a fine-tuned Qwen3-32B teacher model), which could become a resource bottleneck when scaling up training runs.

Results are reported as single-run point estimates without confidence intervals or error bars across random seeds, which would help substantiate statistical significance given the stochasticity of RL exploration and simulated user environments.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Addresses a prevalent and critical failure mode in multi-turn tool-using language agents, where smaller models often get stuck in repetitive invalid invocation loops upon encountering runtime errors.

Sound and innovative training mechanism: The concept of 'fission'—branching failed rollouts into corrective rollouts conditioned on diagnostic feedback within the on-policy RL loop—effectively restores advantage variance and provides targeted positive guidance from failures.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments span multiple model sizes (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B) across three demanding benchmarks (BFCL v4 Multi-Turn, TAU-Bench, and TAU2-Bench), showing consistent gains over standard GRPO, recent RL variants (DAPO, Dr.GRPO, AWPO), and specialized 8B tool agents.

Thoughtful analysis and ablations: The paper provides thorough diagnostic experiments, including compute-matched comparisons (Table 4), decomposition into one-shot vs. error-recovery rates (Figure 3), feedback ablation (Static vs. Dynamic in Table 2), and a cross-domain/non-leakage audit of the Error Simulator (Table 3).
weaknesses: Reliance on privileged ground-truth information during simulation: The Error Simulator takes the ground-truth tool call (tau_gt) as input to formulate diagnostic runtime feedback. Although the authors evaluate non-leakage, having an oracle-informed 32B model generate hints ('parameter status expects value OPEN') creates a semi-supervised curriculum that may not easily translate to domains where ground-truth trajectories or strong teacher models are absent.

Computational and infrastructure overhead: Generating G' additional rollouts for error cases alongside querying an external 32B simulator introduces non-trivial wall-clock and GPU memory overhead during training. While update-matched results are reported, total training wall-clock time and simulator inference FLOPs are not reported.

Limited model architecture diversity: Evaluation is restricted solely to the Qwen3 family (1.7B to 8B). Testing across distinct open model families (such as Llama-3 or Mistral) would have strengthened claims regarding framework generalizability.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and acute problem in agentic tool use: the tendency of smaller LLMs to enter repetitive hallucination loops after tool execution errors, and the failure of standard RL (e.g., GRPO) to provide actionable corrective supervision.

The proposed FISSION-GRPO framework is conceptually sound, transforming sparse negative outcomes into dense, on-policy recovery trajectories via dynamic context expansion and group-relative reinforcement learning.

Thorough empirical evaluation across multiple model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) on multiple standard multi-turn benchmarks (BFCL v4, TAU-Bench, and TAU2-Bench), demonstrating consistent and significant gains over standard GRPO and recent variants (DAPO, Dr.GRPO, AWPO).

Compelling control experiments and ablations, specifically isolating the structural effect of fission from the quality of the error simulator (Fission-Static vs. Fission-Dynamic), verifying compute-matched parity, and evaluating simulator generalization and target leakage.
weaknesses: The framework introduces operational complexity and training overhead by requiring an in-the-loop 32B Error Simulator to generate dynamic diagnostics for filtered rollouts during RL training, which may limit practical adoption in resource-constrained training environments.

The 630 seed training instances were synthesized grounded in BFCL characteristics; while generalization to TAU-Bench and TAU2-Bench is tested, a more explicit analysis of tool schema overlap between the synthetic data and BFCL evaluation sets would strengthen the claims.

The error filtering relies on a hard threshold (delta_corr = 1), treating any non-perfect trajectory as an error; sensitivity to this threshold and handling of partially correct multi-call turns could be explored further.
